posts.text:
This week: Kyiv's deadliest night in months. A funeral crossing the Iran–Iraq border. Quakes redrawing Venezuela's coast. Sudan's war rolling east. And UK politicians quietly gaming the breakup of Britain.

5 ways the map moved — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Russia hit Kyiv with its "most massive" attack of the war — at least 30 dead (BBC). Putin toured the front vowing to take more of Ukraine, yet NYT analysts say his wider offensive has stalled and Crimea is buckling under drone strikes, fuel shortages and blackouts.

2/ Iran began a six-day funeral for Ayatollah Khamenei, killed in February at the war's outset. His body will pass through 5 cities in Iran AND Iraq — a state procession across an international border, expected to draw millions. (BBC, Guardian, AJ, DW, NYT)

3/ Twin earthquakes tore through Venezuela's northern coast: makeshift morgues, a tourist town in rubble — and a man pulled alive from a collapsed car park after 8 days. The map changed by geology, not politics. (BBC, Guardian, AJ, NYT)

4/ Amnesty says Sudan's RSF committed crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing at El Fasher (Guardian). An ex-UN official warns El Obeid — the gateway between Darfur and Khartoum — "could be worse" (AJ). The front line is rolling east toward the Nile.

5/ The Guardian reports leaders in Scotland, Wales, NI and Ireland have begun planning for a possible breakup of the UK if Reform UK wins power. Nothing has changed on the ground — but a 300-year-old union is being war-gamed as negotiable.

The parallel: in 1920, Trianon stripped Hungary of two-thirds of its territory. Mapmakers asked what that would look like for Britain — Scotland to Norway, the northeast to Germany, Ireland united, the south coast to France.

A hypothetical. This week it felt less abstract.
